Area of applicability of a spatial prediction model

Source: R/area-of-applicability.R
area_of_applicability.Rd

Computes the dissimilarity index (DI) of Meyer & Pebesma (2021) for a set of prediction locations and flags those that fall inside the model's area of applicability (AOA), the region of predictor space where the model's cross-validated performance estimate can be expected to hold.

Usage

area_of_applicability(
  newdata,
  model = NULL,
  train_sf = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  weights = "auto",
  folds = NULL,
  threshold = NULL,
  normalizer_max_n = 5000L,
  seed = 123L,
  chunk_size = NULL,
  use_fnn = requireNamespace("FNN", quietly = TRUE),
  coords = c("auto", "yes", "no"),
  categorical = c("refuse", "indicator", "drop")
)

Arguments

newdata

Prediction locations: an sf object (typically from predict_surface) or a data.frame, carrying the predictor columns. When location is measured (a gwr_fit, a bayesian_fit, a forest fitted with include_coords = TRUE, or coords = "yes") an sf object is required, non-POINT geometry is reduced to representative points, and a CRS mismatch with the training data is reconciled; see Models whose predictions depend on location.

model

A fitted spatial_fit, supplying the training data and predictor names, the importance weights = "auto" reads, and whether its predictions depend on location. Optional if train_sf and predictor_vars are given directly, which lets this be used with any model.

train_sf

Training data, if not taken from model.

predictor_vars

Predictor names, if not taken from model.

weights

"auto" (default), NULL, or a named numeric vector of predictor importances. "auto" uses pmax(model$info$importance, 0) when model carries a finite importance with at least one positive value, naming every predictor in use, from a model with out-of-bag skill; otherwise every predictor counts equally and a logged note says why (see Weights). NULL is the explicit request for equal weights. For a vector of your own, any positive scale works. When model was fitted with include_coords = TRUE, the coordinates "..x" and "..y" are measured as predictors too (see below), and you are not expected to supply importances for them: any you leave out default to the mean of the weights you did supply, so location counts about as much as a typical predictor. Naming them explicitly overrides that. An unnamed vector may have one value per predictor either with or without the two coordinate columns. Weights must be finite and non-negative, so pass permutation importance as pmax(importance, 0). (A forest with no out-of-bag rows, replace = FALSE with sample_fraction = 1, has NaN importance, which pmax() keeps and which is refused when passed by hand; "auto" uses equal weights for it.) pmax(importance, 0) is all zero when the model found no predictor useful, and then the weights cannot say anything: with a single predictor any weight gives the same index and zero is accepted; with several, all of them are weighted equally, as with weights = NULL, and a warning says so. The coordinate default above is the mean of the supplied weights, so a zero weight on the only covariate of a coordinate-using model zeroes the coordinates too, and that equal weighting applies.

folds

Cross-validation folds: a make_folds result, a list of train/test splits, or a vector of fold labels with one entry per training row. Default NULL (plain nearest neighbour). The folds you passed to cv_*(), built on the layer model was fitted from, may name rows that prep_model_data() removed (a missing or non-finite value, an empty geometry): as in cv_*(), they are dropped from the folds, and a label vector with one entry per row of that layer loses theirs. Also as in cv_*(), a make_folds() result built on other data – another layer, or these rows in another order – is refused. That check is skipped when the folds were built on polygons and the training data are the points a fit reduced them to.

threshold

Optional numeric override for the DI threshold of the predictor index. The location index, when there is one, always takes its threshold from the rule.

normalizer_max_n

Subsample the training data to this many points when computing the mean pairwise distance, which is quadratic. Default 5000.

seed

Seed for that subsample. Default 123.

chunk_size

Query rows per distance block on the dense path. Default NULL (chosen from the training size). Otherwise a single number of at least 1; a fractional value is truncated to a whole number of rows.

use_fnn

Use FNN for nearest-neighbour search when available. Exposed so the dense fallback can be tested. The two paths return the same distances: the dense one searches with a fast formula and then recomputes the nearest distance exactly, so an exact copy of a training row is at distance 0 on both.

coords

Whether location is measured: "auto" (default) measures it for a model whose predictions depend on it (a gwr_fit, a bayesian_fit, a forest fitted with include_coords = TRUE) and not otherwise; "yes" measures it whatever the model, and with no model; "no" never does, and logs a caution for a model that depends on it. See Models whose predictions depend on location.

categorical

What to do with factor and character predictors: "refuse" (default) stops with a message naming them and the two alternatives; "indicator" codes each level as a 0/1 column and marks a prediction row on a level no training row has as outside (DI = Inf); "drop" computes the index on the other predictors and logs which were left out. See Limitations for the scaling "indicator" uses.

Value

An object of class aoa: a list with

  • aoa: newdata with a numeric DI column and a logical AOA column added, and between them a numeric DI_location column when location has an index of its own. For a forest fitted with include_coords = TRUE it is the object the computation ran on: newdata after pointizing, CRS reconciliation and the addition of the "..x" and "..y" columns. With a location index it is newdata as passed. A row whose predictors are not all finite gets NA in DI, and a row outside the training range of a predictor in dropped_vars, or on a level no training row has, gets DI = Inf and AOA = FALSE (see Limitations). AOA is DI <= threshold, and with a location index also DI_location <= location$threshold: a row outside on either index is FALSE, and a row with one index missing and the other inside is NA.

  • threshold: the DI cut-off used.

  • train_DI: the training points' own DI values.

  • normalizer: the mean pairwise training distance.

  • weights: the weight vector actually applied, named by predictor_vars.

  • predictor_vars: the predictors used, including "..x"/"..y" when a forest uses the coordinates and excluding dropped_vars and, under categorical = "drop", categorical_vars.

  • dropped_vars: predictors dropped for negligible variance.

  • scaling: a list with center and scale, each named by predictor_vars: the training means and standard deviations the index is computed in, so a location's DI can be traced to the predictor that put it outside. A predictor coded as indicators has one entry per level, named "<predictor>=<level>".

  • n_outliers: the number of training DI values above the Q3 + 1.5 * IQR fence, which the default threshold rule sets aside (the "outlier-removed" in its name); computed whether or not threshold was supplied.

  • n_duplicates: with folds = NULL, the number of training rows that repeat an earlier row's predictor values exactly and so share its reference distance; NA when folds were supplied (see Training rows with identical predictor values).

  • location: NULL, or for a location index a list with threshold, train_DI, normalizer (the mean distance between training points, in map units, so threshold * normalizer is the cut-off as a distance), n_duplicates (training rows at an earlier row's location; NA when folds were supplied) and n_outside (prediction rows beyond the location threshold).

  • categorical_vars: the factor and character predictors found, coded or left out as params$categorical says.

  • n_train, n_new, n_inside, n_outside, n_na: row counts. n_train counts the training rows that survived the finite-value filter; n_new is every row of newdata, so n_new = n_inside + n_outside + n_na, with n_na the rows whose AOA is NA. n_outside_predictors counts the rows beyond the predictor threshold, which is n_outside unless there is a location index.

  • params records the call: folds_supplied, n_folds, folds_method, threshold_supplied, normalizer_max_n, normalizer_n_used, normalizer_subsampled, weights_supplied (the caller passed a vector), weights_source ("model importance", "supplied" or "equal"), weights_note (the kind of importance, or why the weights are equal), coords ("location index", "predictors" or "none"), categorical and seed. folds_method is the method of a make_folds() result ("block_kfold", "random_kfold", ...), "labels" for a vector of fold labels, "splits" for a bare list of train/test splits, and NA when no folds were supplied. It is printed with the object, because the threshold's meaning depends on it: the cross-validated DI that sets it comes from the same kind of hold-out as the CV error it should be quoted beside, so an AOA built on random_kfold folds is logged as a caution and does not belong next to a blocked cv_*() result.

Why a map alone is not enough

A fitted model will return a number for any location you hand it, including locations whose predictor values look nothing like anything it was trained on. Those predictions are extrapolations dressed as interpolations, and a cross-validation score says nothing about them, because the held-out folds were drawn from the same predictor distribution as the training data. The AOA marks where the score applies.

How it is computed

Predictors are centred and scaled using the training data's own means and standard deviations, then weighted by variable importance when the model carries one (see Weights). For a prediction point \(p\), the DI is the distance to its nearest training point in that space, divided by the mean pairwise distance among training points. The same quantity is computed for the training data itself, using each point's nearest neighbour among the training rows of the fold that holds it out. That means everything outside its own fold for random and block folds, and the smaller training set that buffered and NNDM folds actually leave (see The fold scheme changes the answer); without folds it is the nearest training row with different predictor values. The threshold is then the largest training DI that is not an upper outlier, i.e. not above the fence Q3 + 1.5 * IQR of the training DI, with the quartiles of stats::quantile()'s default type 7. Prediction points at or below that threshold are inside the AOA.

That is the paper's "outlier-removed maximum". CAST, the reference implementation, computes the same fence with the same quartiles but uses the fence itself as the threshold, capped at the largest training DI. The two agree whenever no training DI lies above the fence (n_outliers is 0); otherwise CAST's threshold is the larger, and so is its AOA. (Earlier CAST releases used grDevices::boxplot.stats(), which gives the rule used here but with Tukey's hinges as the quartiles, so they can also differ when the number of training points is even.) To apply the current CAST rule to the same training DI, pass threshold = min(quantile(res$train_DI, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR(res$train_DI), max(res$train_DI)) for an earlier result res.

The DI is invariant to the overall scale of weights: the numerator and the normaliser carry the same factor. Importance values can be passed as-is.

Training rows with identical predictor values

Repeat visits to a site with static covariates, or covariates read off a raster coarser than the sampling, give training rows that are exact copies of each other in predictor space. A copy is the same point of that space, not a neighbour. Counted as a neighbour it gives a training DI of 0, and once about three quarters of the rows have one the threshold is 0 and only exact copies of a training row count as inside (60 sites visited 4 times put 30 of 200 new points inside; the same sites counted once put 188).

With folds = NULL each training row's reference is therefore its nearest row with different values: the search runs on the distinct rows and every row takes its point's distance. n_duplicates counts the rows that repeat an earlier one, and a layer with none is computed exactly as before. The normaliser stays the mean pairwise distance over all the training rows, so a prediction point's DI is the same with and without folds.

With folds supplied the definition is applied as it stands: a held-out row whose copy is on the training side of its fold has a DI of 0, because that hold-out did have an identical row to learn from. If the threshold comes out 0 that way, a warning of class spatialkit_aoa_zero_threshold gives the count, so a script or a cross-validation loop can catch it with tryCatch(..., spatialkit_aoa_zero_threshold = ). Folds that keep the copies together (make_folds(method = "leave_location_out", group_var = ...)) give the threshold its meaning back. The same applies to the location index when training rows share a location.

The fold scheme changes the answer, and should

With folds = NULL the training reference is each point's nearest neighbour anywhere in the training data, which for clustered data is very close, giving a small threshold and a conservative AOA. Passing the folds you actually validated with makes the reference distances larger and the AOA correspondingly wider. That is not a loophole. The AOA is defined relative to a performance estimate, and a spatially blocked estimate is a claim about predicting further away. Pass the same make_folds() result you passed to cv_spatial. Buffered and NNDM folds use the training set they actually left available, not merely "everything outside the fold".

Weights

Meyer and Pebesma weight the predictors by the model's variable importance, and with the default weights = "auto" so does this function whenever model carries an importance that means something: pmax(model$info$importance, 0), which a forest from fit_rf_model has. Equal weights are used, with a logged note, when it does not: no model; a model with no importance (importance = "none", a GWR, a Bayesian fit); an importance that is not finite (NaN for a forest with no out-of-bag rows); one that names fewer predictors than are in use; no positive value; or a forest with no out-of-bag skill (oob_r_squared missing or at most 0), whose positive importances are noise. print() says which it was. weights = NULL asks for equal weights whatever the model carries.

What the weights buy: with 2 predictors the forest uses and 8 it does not, equal weights put about 70\ (4 times the in-sample RMSE) inside the AOA and importance weights about 26\ 43\ so its square enters the distance, and a weak but real predictor is down-weighted by the square of its relative importance. A shift along one can then go unseen (94\ test, against 19\ weights = sqrt(pmax(importance, 0)) is the gentler alternative: it kept most of the gain on used predictors and put 46\ shift inside, at the cost of 77\ shifts.

Limitations

Categorical predictors (factor or character columns) have no distance of their own, and by default they are refused and never silently dummy-coded. categorical = "indicator" codes each level that occurs in the training rows as a 0/1 column. The columns of one predictor share one scale, sqrt(1 - sum(p^2)) with p the levels' shares of the training rows, so two rows on different levels are the same distance apart whichever levels they are, two on the same level are 0 apart, and the predictor adds as much to the mean squared distance between training rows as one standardised numeric predictor. That scaling is a choice, not a result, which is why it is not the default. A prediction row on a level no training row has gets DI = Inf, is outside the AOA, and a warning gives the count. categorical = "drop" leaves the categorical predictors out and computes the index on the others; a level the training data never has then goes unseen.

Predictors whose variance is negligible relative to their own magnitude (the test is sd < sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) * max(abs(x)), so the same variable in metres and in gigametres is treated identically) are dropped from the distance. A prediction point taking a value there outside the training range (with the same relative tolerance) is extrapolation along a direction the training data never varied in: its scaled distance along it is infinite, so it gets DI = Inf, is outside the AOA, and a warning gives the count. A point missing that value is judged on the other predictors. With equal weights every predictor counts the same, which overstates dissimilarity along directions the model barely uses; see Weights.

Models whose predictions depend on location

For three kinds of model the prediction is a function of where the point is, not only of its covariates, so the index has to measure location too. Without that a prediction point far outside the training extent but with ordinary covariate values reads as inside the area of applicability, which is exactly the extrapolation this index exists to catch. coords = "auto" (the default) measures location for all three; coords = "no" turns it off, with a logged caution; coords = "yes" measures it for any model, or for none.

A geographically weighted regression (gwr_fit) has coefficients that vary over the map, and a Bayesian spatial model (bayesian_fit) has a Gaussian-process term in the coordinates. For these, and under coords = "yes", location gets an index of its own, built like the predictor index but in map space: DI_location is the distance to the nearest training point over the mean distance between training points; the training points' own values use the same folds; and the threshold is the same outlier-removed maximum. A prediction point is inside the AOA only if it is inside on both indices, and both DI columns are returned so the cause can be read off. Location is kept apart from the covariates because, as two more equally weighted columns, it is diluted as covariates are added: with 12 of them, 89\ beyond a 1000-unit training extent still read as inside, against none with the separate index. In a test with a GWR whose slope rises eastward, points one half to one and a half extents beyond the data had 13 times the in-extent RMSE; 84\ with location measured.

Inside the extent the index marks an unsampled gap only where the gap is wider than the distance its threshold allows, and that distance depends on folds. With folds = NULL it is the spacing of the training points (the outlier-removed largest nearest-neighbour distance). With blocked folds it is the largest distance from a held-out point to the nearest row its fold trained on, outliers removed, which grows with the block size; a gap narrower than about twice that distance has no cell beyond it and reads as inside. In a test with 400 training points in two strips 400 units apart, the cut-off without folds was 46 to 54 units and no grid cell in the middle half of the gap, 100 units or more from either strip, was inside. That held although the prediction grid took its covariates from the nearest observation, so that every cell's covariate DI was 0. With five block folds the cut-off was 199 to 251 units and 76 to 100\ three draws). This follows from the definition and is not a fault of the index: the cross-validated error it is paired with was earned on hold-outs that far from their training rows. It does mean that with blocked folds the location index says nothing about a gap narrower than about twice the cut-off; location$threshold * location$normalizer is the cut-off in map units, and print() shows it.

A forest fitted with include_coords = TRUE splits on the coordinates like on any other column, so there they join the predictor index as "..x" and "..y" and are centred, scaled and weighted with the rest.

Either way geometry is needed on both sides, so train_sf and newdata must both be sf objects; a data.frame is refused rather than quietly measured without location. Non-POINT newdata (grid polygons, say) is reduced to representative points first, as coerce_to_points would. If exactly one side carries a CRS the other is brought into it: reprojected when its coordinates look like longitude/latitude, stamped otherwise, with a warning either way. This is done because degrees fed into a metre-space index silently understate the distances. The location index is a map distance and refuses training data in a geographic CRS.

References

Meyer, H. and Pebesma, E. (2021). Predicting into unknown space? Estimating the area of applicability of spatial prediction models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 12(9), 1620–1633. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13650

See also

predict_surface to build the grid, make_folds for the fold scheme.

Other cross-validation: cv_bayes(), cv_block_size_sweep(), cv_gwr(), cv_rf(), cv_spatial(), estimate_sac_range(), fold_separation(), gwr_model_selection(), make_folds(), sac_nugget(), select_features_forward()

Other prediction: predict_surface()

Examples

library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.12.1, GDAL 3.8.4, PROJ 9.4.0; sf_use_s2() is TRUE
set.seed(1)
n <- 120
train <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
             a = rnorm(n), b = rnorm(n)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
train$z <- 2 * train$a - train$b + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

# Prediction points, some of them well outside the training predictor range
newpts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(50, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(50, 0, 1000),
             a = c(rnorm(40), rnorm(10, 8)), b = rnorm(50)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)

res <- area_of_applicability(newpts, train_sf = train,
                             predictor_vars = c("a", "b"))
res
#> Area of applicability (Meyer & Pebesma 2021)
#> 
#>   predictors  : 2 (a, b)
#>   weighted    : no (all predictors count equally: no model was given)
#>   training    : 120 points
#>   reference   : nearest other training point (no folds supplied)
#>   normaliser  : 1.7777 (mean pairwise distance)
#>   threshold   : 0.2899 (outlier-removed max of training DI)
#>   location    : not measured
#> 
#>   39 of 50 prediction points inside the AOA (78.0%)
#> 
#> Predictions outside the AOA are extrapolations; the cross-validated
#> performance estimate does not cover them.
table(res$aoa$AOA)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>    11    39
